q: Ethyl benzoate is treated with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in ether, followed by aqueous workup. What are the organic products?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> delivers hydride twice to an ester. What happens to the OR group?
w: The first hydride gives a tetrahedral intermediate that expels ethoxide, forming benzaldehyde. The aldehyde is more reactive than the ester and is reduced at once by a second hydride. Workup protonates both alkoxides: benzyl alcohol (PhCH2OH) and ethanol.
x: Benzaldehyde is an intermediate, but with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> it is reduced further to the primary alcohol.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent; it does not hydrolyze the ester to the acid.
The C–O bond to the acyl carbon is broken and the ethoxy group leaves; the oxygen is not retained as an ether link.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride. At −78 °C the tetrahedral intermediate does not collapse until workup.
w: One equivalent of DIBAL-H at −78 °C adds one hydride to the ester; the aluminum-bound tetrahedral intermediate is stable at that temperature, so no aldehyde is present while active hydride remains. Aqueous workup collapses it to A, hexanal (plus methanol).
x: Hexan-1-ol is the LiAlH<sub>4</sub> product (or DIBAL-H in excess at room temperature), where the aldehyde is reduced again.
DIBAL-H is a reducing agent; it does not hydrolyze the ester to the acid.
Hydride replaces OCH<sub>3</sub> on the carbonyl carbon; the C=O oxygen is not removed to form an ether.

q: Why must the reduction of an ester to an aldehyde with DIBAL-H be run at −78 °C?
c: The Al-bound tetrahedral intermediate survives at −78 °C and gives the aldehyde only at workup
At −78 °C DIBAL-H attacks only the ester oxygen, not the carbonyl carbon, so it cleaves the C–O bond
At higher temperature DIBAL-H reduces the ester all the way to an alkane, removing both oxygens
At −78 °C the aldehyde product freezes out of solution as it forms, so it is protected
h: The danger is a second hydride addition. What species would have to be present for that to happen?
w: An aldehyde is more reactive than an ester, so if it formed while DIBAL-H was still present it would be reduced to the primary alcohol. At −78 °C the tetrahedral intermediate (O–Al(iBu)2 on carbon, with OR still attached) is stable; it collapses to the aldehyde only during aqueous workup, after the hydride is destroyed.
x: DIBAL-H is a Lewis acid that coordinates to the C=O oxygen, but the hydride is delivered to the carbonyl carbon at any temperature.
The over-reduction product at higher temperature is the primary alcohol; aluminum hydrides do not remove the oxygen to give an alkane.
Selectivity comes from the stability of the tetrahedral intermediate in solution, not from precipitation of the aldehyde.

q: What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: A lactone is a cyclic ester. Reduce it the way you would any ester, then remember both ends belong to one molecule.
w: LiAlH4 reduces an ester to two alcohols: the acyl carbon becomes CH2OH and the alkoxy oxygen becomes an OH. In a lactone both pieces are in one molecule, so the ring opens to A, butane-1,4-diol.
x: The lactol (cyclic hemiacetal) is what one hydride gives, e.g. DIBAL-H at −78 °C; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces on through the open-chain aldehyde.
Tetrahydrofuran would require removing the carbonyl oxygen completely while keeping the ring; hydride reduction does not do that.
Butan-1-ol has lost an oxygen; the ring oxygen is retained as the second OH group.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: A Grignard reagent adds to an ester, the alkoxide leaves, and a ketone forms. Is the ketone more or less reactive than the ester?
w: CH3MgBr adds, methoxide leaves, and acetophenone forms. A ketone is more electrophilic than an ester, so it consumes a second CH3MgBr right away. Workup gives the 3° alcohol with two new methyls: A, 2-phenylpropan-2-ol.
x: Acetophenone is the intermediate; it cannot be stopped at with a Grignard reagent because it reacts faster than the ester.
A secondary alcohol would need one methyl and one hydride; no hydride source is present.
This hemiketal-like structure is the first tetrahedral intermediate; it loses methoxide before workup and is not isolated.

q: Which ester and Grignard reagent (excess, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) give the alcohol shown?
h: An ester + excess RMgBr makes a 3° alcohol with two identical R groups from the Grignard. Which two groups on the carbinol carbon match?
w: The carbinol carbon carries Ph, CH2CH3 and CH2CH3. The two identical groups (two ethyls) come from the Grignard reagent; the different one (phenyl) comes from the ester's acyl group. So methyl benzoate + excess CH3CH2MgBr gives 3-phenylpentan-3-ol.
x: Ethyl propanoate + excess PhMgBr gives two phenyls and one ethyl on the carbinol carbon (1,1-diphenylpropan-1-ol).
Methyl propanoate + excess EtMgBr gives three ethyls (3-ethylpentan-3-ol); there is no phenyl.
Ethyl acetate + excess PhMgBr gives 1,1-diphenylethanol (two phenyls and one methyl).

q: What is the product after aqueous workup?
h: Treat the lactone like any ester: the acyl carbon gets two R groups; the ring oxygen becomes a separate alcohol.
w: The first CH3MgBr adds to the C=O; the tetrahedral intermediate opens the ring, releasing an alkoxide on the far end and leaving a methyl ketone. The ketone adds a second CH3MgBr. Workup protonates both alkoxides: A, 4-methylpentane-1,4-diol.
x: The hydroxy ketone is the intermediate after one addition; with excess Grignard the ketone reacts again.
A cyclic ether would need a separate ring-closing step (e.g. strong acid and heat); the mild workup simply protonates the two alkoxides.
Pentane-1,4-diol has only one methyl on C4 and an H; forming it would require a hydride reduction step.

q: Ethyl formate is treated with excess phenylmagnesium bromide, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. What is the product?
h: A formate ester is HC(=O)OR. The acyl carbon keeps its H.
w: PhMgBr adds to the formyl carbon and ethoxide leaves, giving benzaldehyde. The aldehyde is more reactive than the ester and adds a second PhMgBr. The carbinol carbon carries H, Ph and Ph: A, diphenylmethanol, a secondary alcohol. Formate esters are the one ester that gives 2° rather than 3° alcohols with Grignard reagents.
x: Benzaldehyde is the intermediate; it reacts with the excess Grignard faster than the ester does.
A third phenyl would require replacing the formyl H; the C–H bond is not a leaving group.
Benzyl alcohol would require hydride, not phenyl, to add to benzaldehyde.

q: N-Methylbenzamide is heated at reflux in 6 M HCl for several hours. What species are present at the end, before any neutralization?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond. Then ask what form each product takes in strong acid.
w: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis cleaves the amide C–N bond, giving benzoic acid and methylamine. In 6 M HCl the amine is protonated to methylammonium; this protonation is what makes acidic amide hydrolysis irreversible. The acid stays un-ionized at low pH: benzoic acid and CH3NH3+.
x: Benzoate and free methylamine are the forms present under basic conditions; at low pH the acid is neutral and the amine is protonated.
The methyl group is on nitrogen, not oxygen; hydrolysis cannot transfer it to make a methyl ester.
Hydrolysis does not change the oxidation state of the carbonyl carbon; no aldehyde forms.

h: With amides, LiAlH<sub>4</sub> removes the carbonyl oxygen instead of the nitrogen. Why is N not lost?
w: Hydride adds to the C=O, but the poorer leaving group is the amide nitrogen, so the oxygen (as an O–Al species) is expelled instead, giving an iminium ion. A second hydride reduces the iminium. The C=O becomes CH2 and the carbon count is unchanged: A, N,N-dimethyl(cyclohexylmethyl)amine.
x: Losing the nitrogen to give a primary alcohol is the ester pattern; for amides the oxygen leaves because R<sub>2</sub>N<sup>−</sup> is a far worse leaving group.
An aldehyde is not the product of LiAlH<sub>4</sub> with an amide; the iminium ion that forms is reduced again.
The carbonyl carbon is retained as CH<sub>2</sub>; this structure has lost a carbon.

q: What does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> (then H<sub>2</sub>O) convert the lactam shown into?
h: Amide + LiAlH<sub>4</sub>: C=O → CH<sub>2</sub>, nitrogen kept.
w: LiAlH4 reduces an amide C=O to CH2 and keeps the C–N bond. For a cyclic amide the ring stays closed, so piperidin-2-one becomes A, piperidine.
x: 5-Aminopentan-1-ol would require cleavage of the C–N bond; with amides the oxygen is lost, not the nitrogen.
Pentan-1-amine has lost an oxygen and opened the ring; the ring stays intact because no ring bond to N is cut.
This cyclic hemiaminal still carries an oxygen; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> removes the carbonyl oxygen completely, so it is not the product.

q: N,N-Diethylacetamide is heated at reflux in aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
h: Hydrolysis cuts the C–N bond. What form does each fragment take in strong base?
w: Hydroxide adds to the amide C=O and the C–N bond breaks on prolonged heating. In base, the acid ends up as the carboxylate and the amine as the free amine: sodium acetate and diethylamine.
x: These are the forms under acidic conditions; in NaOH the acid is deprotonated and the amine is neutral.
Hydrolysis breaks the acyl C–N bond; the ethyl groups stay on nitrogen and are not converted to ethanol.
Hydrolysis does not reduce the carbonyl carbon; no aldehyde forms.

q:
Which statements about amides are correct?
I. When an amide is protonated by a strong acid, the proton goes mainly to the oxygen.
II. The C–N bond in an amide is shorter than the C–N bond in an amine.
III. Amides are stronger bases than amines because their nitrogen is sp2 hybridized.
h: Use the C=N resonance form of the amide. Where is the electron density, and is the N lone pair available?
w: Because the N lone pair is delocalized onto oxygen, O is the most basic site: O-protonation gives a cation stabilized by resonance with N (I true). The same delocalization gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so it is shorter (about 1.34 Å vs 1.47 Å in an amine) (II true). Delocalization makes the N lone pair less available, so amides are far weaker bases than amines (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 0 vs ≈ 10) (III false). Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: resonance gives the amide C–N bond partial double-bond character, so it is shorter than an amine C–N single bond.
Statement III is false: the delocalized lone pair makes amides very weak bases, much weaker than amines.
Statement III is false, so all three cannot be correct.

q: Rank the esters in order of increasing rate of hydrolysis with NaOH (slowest first).
h: All three are acetates, so the acyl part is the same. Compare the leaving groups by the pK<sub>a</sub> of their conjugate acids: CH<sub>3</sub>OH 15.5, phenol 10.0, 4-nitrophenol 7.2.
w: The weaker the base that leaves, the better the leaving group, and the more electron-withdrawing the OR group, the more electrophilic the C=O. Methoxide (from CH3OH, pKa 15.5) is the poorest leaving group, phenoxide (10.0) is better, and 4-nitrophenoxide (7.2), stabilized by resonance into NO2, is best. Slowest to fastest: I < II < III. (4-Nitrophenyl esters are used as 'activated esters' for this reason.)
x: This reverses the trend: a more stable (weaker-base) leaving group makes hydrolysis faster, not slower.
Phenoxide is a better leaving group than methoxide because its negative charge is delocalized into the ring, so phenyl acetate reacts faster than methyl acetate.
The para-nitro group stabilizes the phenoxide by resonance, making it the best leaving group, so III is fastest.

h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild hydride donor. Which carbonyl is more electrophilic: a ketone or an ester?
w: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones readily but reacts only very slowly with esters, whose C=O is stabilized by resonance donation from the OCH3 oxygen. Only the ketone is reduced: A, methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate (racemic).
x: Reducing the ester while leaving the ketone reverses the reactivity order; ketones are more reactive than esters.
Reducing both carbonyls is the LiAlH<sub>4</sub> result; NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce the ester.
Converting C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> requires Wolff–Kishner or Clemmensen conditions, not NaBH<sub>4</sub>.
